rejected.title: Converse and equivalence
card: The converse of "if P then Q" swaps the two parts to give "if Q then P". Neither part is changed or negated. Example: "If a shape is a square, then it has four sides" has the converse "If a shape has four sides, then it is a square".
The converse is not always true when the original is true. In the example, a rectangle has four sides but is not a square.
To show a converse is false, find one case where Q is true and P is false. One such case is called a counterexample.
If "if P then Q" and its converse "if Q then P" are both true, then P and Q are equivalent. This is written "P if and only if Q".
rejected.remember: Swapping the parts of a true statement may make it false. If both directions are true, P and Q are equivalent.

a.q: For a whole number n, what is the converse of "If n is divisible by 10, then n is divisible by 5"?
opts: If n is divisible by 5, then n is divisible by 10
If n is not divisible by 10, then n is not divisible by 5
If n is not divisible by 5, then n is not divisible by 10
If n is divisible by 10, then n is not divisible by 5
a.why: The converse only swaps the two parts, so it starts with divisible by 5 and ends with divisible by 10. The options with "not" change the parts by negating them, which the converse never does. Swapping and negating both parts gives the contrapositive, a different idea.
a.clue: Swap the two parts without changing either one.

b.q: Which statement about "If x = 3, then x² = 9" and its converse is correct?
opts: The converse is false, because x = −3 gives x² = 9
The converse is true, so x = 3 and x² = 9 are equivalent
The converse is false, because x = 3 does not give x² = 9
The original is false, so the converse cannot be true
b.why: The converse is "If x² = 9, then x = 3". Taking x = −3 gives x² = 9 but x ≠ 3, so this counterexample makes the converse false. The original is true, so P and Q are not equivalent.
b.clue: Look for another number whose square is 9.
